title: Soft-decision sensing lets 1.5 fF capacitors meet target BER
idea: First-principles budget: bitline kT/C noise is only ~0.3 mV against ~100 mV of signal, so most of today's 5 fF of charge is spent on worst-case sense-amp offset and not on thermal noise. Sense each bitline with three staggered trip points (2-bit soft output) and feed log-likelihoods to a rate-0.94 LDPC over 1 KB, letting Cs drop to ~1.5 fF.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): aspect ratio from ~70:1 to ~20:1, which removes deep-etch and high-k steps, for ~15-20% lower cost per bit.

title: In-package deuterium reservoir re-passivates retention-tail traps in field
idea: Tail cells trace to single Si dangling-bond traps whose emission is exponential in field, and Si-D bonds resist depassivation ~10x better than Si-H. A Ti/Pd deuteride film in the package releases D2 during a 150 C self-anneal mode, which starts when the ECC-logged weak-cell count passes a threshold.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3), self-healing: holds the <=13 fA tail through the product's life and allows 2-4x longer refresh in later years.

title: Adiabatic charge-recycling refresh between subarray bitlines
idea: The physical minimum for refresh is the leaked charge times V (~0.1 fJ/bit), yet ~90% of the 46 fJ goes into swinging bitlines (Cbl ~10x Cs). Ramp the bitlines with an N-step adiabatic driver, then pass the charge on the restored bitlines to the next subarray's bitlines over a stepwise charge-share bus, so each refresh reuses ~70% of the previous swing.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): ~46 fJ/bit to ~12 fJ/bit, a 10-20% cut in idle power.

title: Per-row leaky charge-bucket counts activations beside wordline driver
idea: Row hammer is a counting threshold (~1k ACTs). Each ACT dumps a fixed charge packet from the wordline driver onto a tiny per-row floating integrator, which leaks with a time constant equal to the refresh window. When its voltage crosses a comparator level, the neighbor rows are flagged for refresh. The result is an exact per-row analog counter instead of SRAM/CAM tables.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): per-row tracking for <1% area, which closes the sampling gaps that TRRespass-style patterns exploit.

title: Unidirectional error codes matched to one-way charge leakage
idea: Retention physics is one-way: a charged node can only lose electrons, so true-cells fail 1->0 and anti-cells fail 0->1, never the reverse. After de-scrambling cell polarity, apply Bose-Lin/Borden t-unidirectional-error-correcting codes. They need far fewer check bits than symmetric BCH for the same t.
why: Retention tail/ECC overhead: parity drops from 6.25% to ~3%, or 2x the correction at equal overhead, which allows longer refresh.

title: Charge-minimizing inversion coding keeps bits in non-leaking state
idea: Only the charged state decays, so the error rate scales with the fraction of charged cells. A per-32-bit codebook flag (bus-invert style, aware of true/anti polarity) stores each chunk so that >=65% of cells sit in the discharged state.
why: Retention errors/refresh: exposure to tail failures roughly halved, which permits ~2x longer refresh with the same ECC, plus lower write energy.

title: Sub-ambient coolant loop priced against Arrhenius refresh savings
idea: Tail leakage has Ea ~0.6-0.9 eV, so retention doubles every ~8-10 C, and dropping junctions from 85 C to 25 C buys ~60-100x retention. Route 10 C facility water to the memory cold plates first, and let on-die sensors stretch refresh to 1-4 s.
why: Refresh (fact 3): recovers the 16-33% of idle power and 10-20% of bandwidth spent on refresh, and lets weaker binned dies pass.

title: Buried high-SRH recombination layer absorbs row-hammer electrons
idea: Part of the hammer disturbance is electrons injected by the aggressor that diffuse through the substrate to victim junctions. Implant a carbon- or gold-doped layer deep below the storage-junction depletion region, where short minority lifetime (<1 ns) kills the migrating electrons. Keeping it out of the depletion region avoids raising SRH generation leakage.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): could push the flip threshold from ~1k toward ~10k ACTs, with no controller logic.

title: Erasure-coded subarrays give on-die chipkill at 3x defect density
idea: Die yield follows exp(-A*D0). Spare rows fix point defects, but one dead subarray or sense-amp stripe kills the die. Stripe each access across 18 subarrays as RS(18,16) symbols, so any two dead subarrays are erased by fuse map.
why: Yield/capital: die yield ~60% to ~90% at the same D0, so fabs can ship from less mature, cheaper tools and ramp faster. Costs 12.5% of bits.

title: Poisson-tail-derived scrubbing replaces 64 ms refresh
idea: Fit the measured retention distribution and compute the expected failures per 1 KB row at a 1 s interval (~0.5). Choose BCH t=6 per row so P(uncorrectable) < 1e-18, then replace blanket refresh with a read-correct-writeback scrub every 1 s.
why: Refresh (fact 3): ~15x less refresh energy and bandwidth, and tail cells become acceptable rather than repaired.

title: Lifetime-tagged refresh-free banks for short-lived tensors
idea: A bit needs refresh only if it must outlive its charge. Compiler/runtime tags allocations with predicted lifetime, and activations, gradient buffers and per-step scratch (<20 ms) go to banks with refresh disabled. A per-region birth-time register faults any read past the retention deadline.
why: Refresh on AI parts: removes refresh from 30-60% of the footprint, and dies with weak retention become sellable as scratch tier.

title: Slow-edge two-level wordline precharge stops trap charge pumping
idea: One hammer mechanism is charge pumping: each ACT/PRE swing fills and empties interface traps under the aggressor or passing gate, emitting electrons toward the victim. Pumped charge per cycle falls when the falling edge is slower than trap emission time. A two-step precharge with a ramped edge (~ns) keeps trap occupancy near equilibrium.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): targets the pumping component, aiming for >5x higher ACT threshold and less TRR overhead.

title: Adaptive twin-cell pairing retires weak cells into differential bits
idea: When test or field ECC finds a weak cell, a fuse pairs it with its neighbor as a 2T2C differential bit sensed on complementary bitlines. Differential sensing doubles the signal and cancels common-mode leakage, so the tail cell stops limiting refresh. The cost is about 0.1% of capacity.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): refresh is set by the 0.1% tail rather than the 1e-9 tail, for ~2-4x longer intervals.

title: Canary replica cells at 60% Cs set local refresh
idea: Each subarray carries 64 deliberately weakened canary cells (60% of nominal Cs, written '1'). They see the same temperature, voltage, VRT and aging as the array but fail first. Background logic polls them, and the subarray's refresh rate relaxes until a canary fails, then steps up.
why: Refresh guardband (fact 3): physical tracking replaces worst-case margins, for 2-4x fewer refreshes.

title: High-field leakage fingerprint screens tail cells in seconds
idea: Tail cells are single traps with field-enhanced (Poole-Frenkel/trap-assisted tunneling) emission, so their leakage climbs steeply with junction field while normal cells barely change. At sort, write '1', raise the plate/substrate bias for 10 ms and read back. Failing cells are the would-be 64 ms tail and get mapped for repair or binning.
why: Test capital/time: replaces hours of retention bake with seconds per die and yields a per-row retention map for relaxed refresh.

title: Relaxed-grade DRAM SKU recovers spec-failing dies with ECC firmware
idea: Dies that fail retention or VRT spec today are scrapped or sold as low grade. Validate them for 32 ms per-row refresh plus host BCH, then sell them 30-40% cheaper with a qualified controller firmware profile to hyperscalers for KV-cache and cache tiers.
why: Usable supply: +5-10% sellable bits from wafers already in the fab, available immediately.

title: JEDEC raw-BER memory class with mandatory host code
idea: Propose a JEDEC/OCP device class specified by raw bit-error rate (e.g., <=1e-6 per bit per second) instead of all-cell 64 ms retention. In exchange, the host must implement a defined end-to-end code and scrub rate.
why: Supply/yield/cost: lets fabs ship dies that fail the old retention screen and accept weaker cells, for a few % to 10%+ more bits per wafer.

title: Row-wide product code computed at activation exploits overfetch
idea: Every ACT already senses a full 8 Kb row (128x overfetch), so all bits sit in the sense amps for free. Place a 2D product code (row checksum plus column parity over 64x128 tiles) in the sense-amp stripe and correct multi-bit clusters before the column read.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) becomes reliability: code rate ~97% vs 94%, and clustered weak-cell failures get corrected.

title: Sense-amp latch timing as analog victim-row health monitor
idea: Sense-amp regeneration time scales as ln(1/signal), so a time-to-digital converter on a few sense amps per mat measures the row's remaining charge at every activation. Rows whose latch time drifts above a threshold are losing charge to hammer, VRT or tail leakage, and get a targeted refresh.
why: Row hammer and VRT (facts 3, 9): detects disturbance by its effect, so any ACT pattern is caught, with no counters.

title: One end-to-end code replaces on-die ECC, link CRC, host ECC
idea: DDR5 pays separately for on-die SEC (6.25%), link CRC and host SECDED/chipkill. Shannon does not care where the noise enters. Encode once at the host with one long code, store it raw, and decode at the host using soft information from the link.
why: Periphery/overhead (fact 7): recovers ~6% die area and energy while correcting more errors.

title: Hadamard-spread weight storage turns bit flips into tiny noise
idea: One exponent or MSB flip in BF16/INT8 weights can wreck a model, which forces DRAM-grade BER. Store each block of 64 weights after a 64-point Walsh-Hadamard transform, invertible in the accelerator for <1% compute. A single stored-bit flip then spreads as +/-delta/8 across 64 weights, below model noise.
why: Error tolerance: inference weights can live at raw BER ~1e-6, i.e., ~10x slower refresh or weak dies, for most AI memory footprint.

title: Compress-then-protect: compression slack carries strong ECC
idea: Real 64 B lines have entropy well below 512 bits (zeros, pointers, small integers; 1.5-2x compressible with BDI/FPC). The controller compresses each line and fills the freed bits with BCH parity up to t=8. Incompressible lines fall back to normal SEC.
why: Retention/weak cells: strong correction for ~70% of lines at zero capacity cost, so refresh can relax ~4x.

title: Drop array voltage to 0.6 V, buy margin with ECC
idea: Restore energy goes as CV^2, so the true optimum is minimum (restore + decode) energy, not zero raw errors. Run VARY at 0.6 V (2.8x less CV^2), accept raw BER ~1e-5 from the reduced signal, and correct with a 2-error code in the base die.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): ~2x lower array and refresh energy.

title: Read-verify-only refresh for non-destructive gain cells
idea: With no capacitor, a 2T/3T gain cell stores the bit on the read transistor's gate and reads it non-destructively as current. Refresh becomes a cheap read scan against a 'decay-warning' threshold set above the decision level, and only the ~0.1-1% of cells crossing it are rewritten.
why: Refresh (fact 3): energy scales with decaying cells, not all cells, so 46 fJ/bit falls to a few fJ/bit and bandwidth is freed.

title: Write-timestamp decay model slides gain-cell read thresholds
idea: Storage-gate voltage in a gain cell decays along a self-limiting, near-logarithmic subthreshold curve, V(t) ~ V0 - S*log10(1+t/tau). Store a 6-bit write epoch per row and place the read reference at the model's predicted midpoint for that age. The deterministic decay is then removed, and only the stochastic spread uses margin.
why: Capacitorless retention: refresh intervals 5-10x longer, so weak gain cells become acceptable.

title: Pilot cells in every row calibrate multilevel gain-cell reads
idea: This borrows pilot tones from wireless. Each 512-cell row carries 8 pilot gain cells written to known levels together with the data, and on read their currents reveal that row's decay, temperature and read-transistor drift. The ADC thresholds are interpolated from the pilots.
why: Density/reliability: 2 bits/cell in capacitorless gain cells despite drift, for 1.5% overhead.

title: Coulomb-blockade nanodot node suppresses leakage by charging energy
idea: A ~2 nm Si nanodot has C ~0.2 aF, so the single-electron charging energy e^2/2C ~0.4 eV ~15 kT, and every escape is penalized by ~exp(-15) on top of the tunnel barrier. Store a bit as N vs N+k electrons, sense with an SET-like gain stage, and vote across 3 dots per bit.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and density: ~1e6x leakage suppression in principle, with no capacitor at all.

title: Goto-pair Esaki tunnel-diode bistable cell needs no refresh
idea: Two series interband tunnel diodes with negative differential resistance (the 1959 Goto pair), rebuilt as stacked SiGe epi under a vertical access transistor, form a bistable node. Retention goes as exp(Eb/kT), so a barrier >40 kT makes it unlimited. The design challenge is a valley current <=1 pA/cell (~5 mW standby per GB).
why: Refresh eliminated (fact 3). Endurance is unlimited because nothing moves atomically. 4-6F^2 without a capacitor.

title: Direct-tunneling germanium nanocrystal trap cell: volatile but wear-free
idea: Charge-trap flash wears out because FN/hot-carrier injection gives electrons enough energy to break oxide bonds. With a 1.5-2 nm tunnel layer, writes at <2 V happen by direct tunneling below the damage threshold. Discrete Ge nanocrystals mean one leaky path drains only one dot. Target ~1 s retention, >1e15 cycles, scrubbed like DRAM.
why: Capacitorless, low-voltage writes, ~15x rarer refresh. Endurance comes from energy-below-damage physics, not from margin.

title: Just-enough-barrier volatile MRAM scrubbed every second
idea: Retention is tau = tau0*e^Delta, and write current scales with Delta. Nonvolatile MRAM over-pays at Delta ~60 kT. Size pMTJs for Delta ~38-40 kT: the per-cell flip probability is ~1e-8 per second, a 1 s ECC scrub catches the rare flips, and the smaller free layer packs denser.
why: Capacitorless, refresh-like scrub at 1 s. Write current -35%, write energy ~-50%, and lower barrier stress gives near-unlimited endurance.

title: Conductive ferroelectric domain-wall cell with non-destructive read
idea: Charged domain walls in LiNbO3/BiFeO3 films conduct 1e3-1e6x more than the bulk. Write by creating or erasing a wall segment between two electrodes with a sub-ns lateral field pulse. Read the wall current without switching polarization, unlike FeRAM's destructive read. The state is polarization topology, so no charge leaks.
why: Destructive read (fact 8) and refresh (fact 3) both removed. Wall pinning, the residual failure mode, is handled by write-verify plus ECC.

title: Read-port-isolated gain cell geometrically immune to read hammer
idea: Hammer needs aggressor toggles to couple into victim storage nodes. In a 3T gain cell, reads toggle only a read wordline on the read transistor's source, and the write wordline moves only on writes (~10x rarer). Shield write wordlines with grounded lines and size node coupling <0.5 mV per toggle, so a flip needs ~1e6 activations.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): threshold from ~1k to ~1M toggles, which removes TRR/counter logic area.

title: E8 lattice coding packs 3 bits/cell in noisy gain cells
idea: Slicing each multilevel cell independently is a cubic lattice and wastes ~3 dB of packing gain. Group 8 gain cells and map 24 bits onto E8 lattice points, the densest packing in 8D, decodable with a few hundred gates. The Voronoi decision regions give 1.5-3 dB more margin against drift.
why: Density: 2 to 3 bits/cell (+50%) with the same capacitorless cells and retention drift.

title: Wide-bandgap floating-body cell where intrinsic carriers vanish
idea: Floating-body cells lose stored holes by SRH generation, which scales with ni ~ exp(-Eg/2kT). 4H-SiC (3.26 eV) has ni ~1e-9 cm^-3 vs 1e10 in Si, ~1e19 lower. Store holes in a p-type SiC or GaN-2DHG floating body under an n-channel, write by band-to-band/impact-ionization pulse, and read by threshold shift.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): from ms toward seconds-hours with no capacitor. SiC substrates have a strong U.S. supply base.

title: Air-gap NEMS relay as zero-leakage gain-cell write switch
idea: The retention tail comes from access-device leakage, and a 10-20 nm gap electrostatic nano-relay has truly zero off-current. Use it only as the write switch of a gain cell, so reads never cycle it and contacts see ~1e10-1e12 cycles over life. The storage gate then holds for hours, limited only by gate tunneling.
why: Refresh (fact 3) essentially removed and the access-transistor tail eliminated, without a capacitor.

title: Buckled-nanobeam bistable bit stores data mechanically
idea: A pre-compressed SiN/SiC nanobeam has two buckled states separated by an elastic barrier of ~1e-18 J (>1e5 kT), so it can't leak or relax. An electrostatic snap-through pulse writes it, a capacitive or piezoresistive gauge reads it non-destructively, and with no contact the elastic cycling exceeds 1e12.
why: Refresh-free, no charge tail, built on a U.S.-native MEMS process. Speed and density still need proof.

title: Atomically uniform hBN barrier collapses gain-cell retention tail
idea: Retention tails come from thickness and trap variation in amorphous oxides, where one extra trap opens a trap-assisted tunneling path. Isolate a 2D storage node (graphene/MoS2) with 5-layer hBN, whose thickness is quantized at 0.33 nm per layer and nearly trap-free, so every cell sees the same barrier.
why: Refresh is set by the median cell instead of a 1e-9 tail cell, for ~100x longer intervals, capacitorless.

title: Series ferroelectric layer makes storage gate self-restoring
idea: Add a thin series ferroelectric to the gain cell's storage gate so the node's charge-voltage curve becomes S-shaped with two wells. Small leakage drifts are resisted until the coercive field, so the node stays latch-like. The bit remains charge-based, unlike a FeFET, which requires full polarization switching.
why: Capacitorless retention: aims for 100x rarer refresh and tolerance of leaky access devices.

title: State-dependent gate capacitance enables global read-free refresh pulse
idea: Gate capacitance differs 2-3x between inversion ('1') and depletion ('0'). A global ratchet pulse train on the read-transistor source couples more charge into '1' nodes than into '0' nodes, and the write device's subthreshold conduction acts as the rectifying pawl. Every row is then refreshed at once with no sensing.
why: Refresh (fact 3): no activates, no sense amps, no bandwidth loss. Energy approaches the leaked-charge minimum.

title: Junctionless storage transistor removes high-field junction leakage tail
idea: In conventional cells the tail is trap-assisted tunneling/GIDL at the high-field n+/p junction. A uniformly doped junctionless thin-body write transistor in a gain cell has no metallurgical junction, so peak field falls 3-5x, and field-enhanced trap emission, which is exponential in field, drops by orders of magnitude.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): ~10x longer refresh in a capacitorless cell.

title: Kirchhoff current-sum parity check scrubs eight rows per read
idea: Gain-cell reads are non-destructive current sources. Opening 8 read wordlines on one bitline sums their currents, and a small ADC returns that column's Hamming weight across 8 rows. Its LSB is checked against a stored column parity.
why: Capacitorless reliability: 8x less scrub energy and bandwidth, so weak cells can be checked often enough.

title: Per-row variable-rate codes from factory cell-quality map
idea: Capacitorless cells spread widely in quality (read-transistor Vt, hole retention). At test, measure each row's raw BER and assign one of 4 code rates (none/SEC/DEC/t=4), stored as a 2-bit map in the controller. Good rows keep full capacity, and bad rows pay parity instead of being scrapped.
why: Yield/usable bits: +10-20% vs fixed worst-case ECC for capacitorless arrays.

title: Deliberate BTI stress re-trims outlier read transistors in field
idea: Bias-temperature instability shifts Vt predictably (dVt ~ t^n, partly permanent). When scrub logs show the same gain cell repeatedly misreading because of a low-Vt read transistor, the controller selects only that cell with a wordline+bitline bias and applies millisecond gate stress, which pushes its Vt back toward the population mean.
why: Self-healing: hard errors are repaired in place with no spares, which keeps capacitorless arrays at full capacity as they age.

title: Write-coalescing plus start-gap rotation qualifies 1e11-endurance cells
idea: First-principles budget: a hot line can take ~2e11 writes in 5 years. An on-die 1 MB write-combining SRAM absorbs >95% of hot rewrites, and start-gap row rotation spreads the rest, so per-cell writes fall below 1e10.
why: Widens the capacitorless menu: charge-trap, volatile MRAM and ferroelectric cells with 1e11-1e12 endurance can serve as DRAM.

title: National open physics-of-failure testbed for capacitorless cells
idea: CHIPS/NIST funds a shared lab that runs standardized retention, disturb, endurance and VRT stresses on any capacitorless cell (gain, floating-body, volatile MRAM, domain-wall). It publishes raw distributions and activation-energy-based acceleration models.
why: U.S. manufacturability/time: each entrant's qualification shrinks from years and ~$50M to months.

title: Licensed gain-cell PDK plus scrub controller for U.S. logic fabs
idea: U.S. logic foundries have no capacitor module but can build BEOL gain cells. A company licenses them a bundle: gain-cell bitcell PDK, drift-compensation/scrub controller IP and a qualification report, for a per-wafer royalty. That turns underused 28-16 nm capacity into capacitorless memory dies.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: no new DRAM fab, so supply comes from existing tools within ~2 years.
